title: Frogs Use Bacteria as Living Armor Against a Deadly Fungus
summary: Some tropical frogs have a natural suit of armor, but it's not made of metal or Kevlar. It's made of bacteria. A new study published in the journal Animal Microbiome shows that certain frog species have bacteria living on their skin that protect them from a deadly fungal disease caused by chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, or Bd). This fungus has already driven at least 90 frog species to extinction and has been found in over 1,300 amphibian species. In amphibians, chytridiomycosis causes skin damage, red skin, convulsions, and eventually heart failure. The fungus is water-borne and spreads through aquatic habitats. "This is one of the clearest demonstrations that a host's natural skin bacteria can be a frontline defense against a pathogen that has devastated amphibian populations globally," said Gui Becker, a study co-author and biologist at Penn State University. To test how skin bacteria protect frogs, researchers conducted a lab experiment in Brazil on two species: Haddadus binotatus and Ischnocnema henselii. They used DNA sequencing to identify the bacteria on each frog's skin. One species, H. binotatus, naturally tolerated the fungus when its healthy skin microbiome was intact. But when the protective bacteria were suppressed with antibiotics, the frogs became more likely to develop signs of disease. The second species, I. henselii, was highly susceptible to the fungus whether or not its microbiome was suppressed. This suggests different frog species rely on different defense strategies. "We see this striking contrast: one species has one of the highest prevalences of the fungus, while the other has no infections in the wild," said Laura Schuck, a study co-author and ecology doctoral student at Penn State. "For years we knew that the tropical frog H. binotatus rarely became infected with the fungus in the wild, but we didn't know why. Now we know." To understand the specific protective mechanisms, Schuck cultured roughly 700 strains of bacteria from the frogs' skin. She grew each strain and exposed the chytrid fungus to the bacteria's chemical byproducts, tracking fungal growth over a week. The team then sequenced each culture and built a custom database linking bacterial identity to how strongly it inhibited the fungus. This database helped identify which disease-inhibiting bacteria were present on each frog's skin. In future studies, the team hopes to learn how frogs acquire protective skin microbiomes from the environment. "If we understand how this frog recruits and maintains beneficial bacteria, we can begin to understand how the microbiome works as a natural defense and what we need to protect in the environment," Schuck said.
why_it_matters: A disease that has already erased dozens of species is being fought by microbes the frogs carry themselves, which could turn ordinary pond mud and leaf litter into a public-health resource for wildlife. It also shows how much conservation now depends on understanding ecosystems at the microscopic level, not just protecting big, visible animals.

background_read: The fungus behind the study, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis — usually shortened to Bd — was only formally identified by scientists in the late 1990s, even though its damage had been building for decades. Since then it has been linked to what researchers describe as the greatest disease-driven loss of biodiversity ever recorded, with amphibian declines documented on every continent where these animals live.

Amphibians (animals such as frogs, toads and salamanders that usually begin life in water and spend part of it on land) are unusually exposed to skin infections, because many of them breathe and absorb water through their skin. When Bd attacks, it thickens the outer skin layer and disrupts the balance of salts in the body — which is why infections can end in heart failure, as the article notes.

Animal Microbiome is a peer-reviewed scientific journal that publishes research on the microscopic communities living on and inside animals. Penn State University (a large public research university in Pennsylvania, in the northeastern United States) is one of the institutions behind the study, and the laboratory work was carried out in Brazil, one of the most frog-rich countries on Earth. The idea that a host's own microbes can act as a first line of defence is now being studied in corals, plants and even human skin.

perspectives.description: If scientists can work out which bacteria block the fungus, they may be able to boost frogs' microbiomes directly — a kind of probiotic for wildlife. The study identifies a natural defence that already exists in the wild, rather than one that has to be invented.

The evidence comes from a lab experiment on two species, and one of them stayed susceptible even with its bacteria intact, so protection is clearly not universal. Suppressing bacteria with antibiotics is also a rough imitation of what happens in nature, so results may not transfer directly to wild populations.

The amphibian chytrid pandemic is a textbook case of a pathogen spreading globally through trade and habitat change, and it shows that host-microbe partnerships are an ancient survival strategy. Different frog species handling the same fungus differently is exactly the variation that drives which species survive an outbreak.

The team's next question — how frogs pick up protective bacteria from their surroundings — points to habitat protection as disease prevention. If the useful microbes live in soil, water or leaf litter, then destroying those habitats removes a defence before anyone notices it is there.
